cards.source_text: - A new study details a deep-sea expedition near the remote Christmas and Cocos islands, where researchers visited unexplored seamounts and identified 149 previously unknown marine species, including black corals, sea worms, sea cucumbers and a variety of fish. - At a site they dubbed “The Shark Tooth Graveyard,” researchers discovered around 1,000 shark teeth, covering more than 22 million years of evolution. - Researchers from institutions in Australia, New Zealand, Canada and the U.S. surveyed the seafloor down to 5,431 meters (17,818 feet), where conditions are cold, dark and high-pressure with limited food options for benthic species. - Deep-sea research is notoriously challenging, but scientists stress the importance of exploring these ecosystems as they face growing threats from warming oceans, pollution, overfishing and deep-sea mining. The Indian Ocean accounts for about a fifth of global ocean area, with 90% of it reaching deeper than 1,000 meters (3,280 feet). Yet compared to the Pacific and Atlantic, its deep-sea biodiversity is relatively understudied — particularly the seamounts of the ocean’s central eastern region. An expedition that surveyed dozens of these volcanic underwater mountains around the Christmas and Cocos islands, located southwest of the Indonesian island of Jakarta between Australia and Sri Lanka, has revealed remarkable marine animal biodiversity along the Indian Ocean seafloor. Published in Deep-Sea Research Part II: Topical Studies in Oceanography in June, the resulting study details 149 new species, including a sea cucumber from the genus Oneirophanta, a new fish from the greeneye family (Chlorophthalmus), and a parasitic barnacle from the genus Rhizolepas. Researchers surveyed at depths ranging from 94 to 5,431 m (308 to 17,818 ft), mapping a dark abyssal seafloor punctuated by 40 to 120-million-year-old volcanic seamounts that can be up to 70 kilometers (43 miles) across. They had never been studied before, study lead author Tim O’Hara, a marine scientist at Museums Victoria in Melbourne, told Mongabay. “People had been around the islands in shallow water before, but no one had looked at life in the deep. It was a massive hole in the data,” O’Hara said. Mapping remote underwater mountains Getting to these sites required time. cards.source_text: At least four suspects have been arrested in connection with the deaths of 18 elephants in the Amboseli ecosystem in southern Kenya, near the border with Tanzania. Preliminary investigations by a multiagency team suggest poisoning from agricultural pesticides, authorities say. In July, 16 elephants were found dead at Kimana Sanctuary and Kuku Group Ranch in the Amboseli ecosystem. The death toll rose to 18 in August, after two more elephant carcasses were found in Kitenden B reserve, near the Amboseli National Park. On Aug. 21, Kenya Wildlife Service’s (KWS) communication director Duncan Wanyama told Mongabay by phone that another elephant was in critical condition in Amboseli and under close watch by animal experts. The KWS has previously said that most of the elephants found dead were female and their calves. Investigations have led to the recovery of substances, including chemicals that are potentially toxic, and “unlabelled materials”, which have been secured for further scientific analysis, Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary for Tourism and Wildlife Rebecca Miano said in a statement seen by Mongabay. “Although the investigations remain active, the arrest of persons of interest and the recovery of exhibits do not in themselves establish criminal culpability,” she said. Miano added that a suspect believed to have crucial information about the killings of the elephants was still at large. Initial investigations indicated that the elephants died after ingesting a toxic substance, with laboratory tests pointing to cyanide. The elephants were thought to have come into contact with the chemical in pesticides sprayed on tomatoes in nearby farms, although Miano said this is yet to be scientifically proven. Farmers from the area have refuted the allegation and told the Associated Press on Aug. 7 that the communities there have long coexisted with elephants. cards.source_text: Hearing the trill or whistle of a bird while going about daily life is well known to boost people’s mood. But a new study suggests the psychological benefits of hearing birdsong are being threatened by traffic noise. Researchers found that even low levels of traffic noise negatively affected the benefits to wellbeing that could otherwise be derived from listening to natural sounds. Bird song has previously been associated with psychological benefits, including stress reduction and positive mood changes, while noise from traffic has been linked to both stress and annoyance. “Bird sounds tend to be one of the elements of nature soundscapes that people perceive as being most relaxing, most pleasant, beneficial for them psychologically,” said Dr Eleanor Ratcliffe, associate professor in environmental psychology at the University of Surrey, and co-author of the study published in People and Nature. The study involved more than 1,500 participants who listened to nine simulated soundscapes consisting of both birdsong and traffic noise and were asked questions about how they made them feel. “We set up the study with the interest of looking at these differences in the objective properties of the soundscape, these levels of acoustic complexity that relate to different levels of biodiversity,” Ratcliffe said. “And our hypothesis was that these would lead to different effects on wellbeing and restoration and stress recovery.” However, listening to birdsong was found to have a psychological benefit, irrespective of its acoustic characteristics. “It shows us that we should support and protect nature for the sake of nature, regardless of whether or not humans have some increased utility benefit from it,” said Ratcliffe. In comparison, the presence of traffic noise negatively affected the psychological benefits of nature’s sounds. Analysis of complementary heart rate measurements on a group of participants showed significantly lower variability for those listening to soundscapes including traffic noise, indicating a greater physiological stress response. The negative effect was found to be more evident when the acoustic characteristics of soundscapes were at high levels, something which may be attributed to overstimulation. Researchers also analysed how differently aged participants responded. cards.source_text: Animal rights campaigners are gearing up for protests and petitions aimed at persuading the French government to ban the hunting of Alpine marmots. Open season on the rodents, members of the squirrel and groundhog family, begins in September, a few weeks before they go into a long winter hibernation. Although the marmot is not a threatened species in France, its numbers are reportedly declining as a result of the climate emergency. Campaigners say they are opposed to them being hunted for fun. Pauline di Nicolantonio, the president of the Association for Justice for Savoie Animals (AJAS), which has launched protests against marmot hunting for the last two years, said: “The question is a moral one. “When you tell people that hunting marmots is allowed in France, they are shocked. The marmot is extremely popular and symbolic in the Savoie where we are based and elsewhere in the Alps. You only have to go into any tourist office to see it’s the main logo or emblem.” Plant-eating marmots are spread across mountainous areas of Europe and North America. Most live in family groups organised by one dominant couple; when threatened they emit a high-pitched signal. In late summer and into autumn their bodies swell to up to 8kg as they stock up on food for a five- to six-month hibernation. There are 15 marmot species in the world and as wild game they were traditionally hunted for their meat, fat and fur. Today, hunting is allowed in certain states in the US and Canada, and in France, Switzerland and Austria but banned in Italy and Germany. An average of 1,000 marmots are shot in France each year. For generations of French children the marmot has been celebrated as the subject of folk tales and poems – one by Goethe set to music by Beethoven – the mascot of Alpine ski resorts and the sympathetic star of a popular television advert for a well-known brand of milk chocolate. In fact, the rodents’ cuddly reputation belies a bloodier reality; much of its waking life is spent in a vicious battle for dominance and territory that often involves killing its parents or children. Christophe Bonenfant, a scientist at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) at the University of Lyon, studies marmots in the Grande Sassière alpine nature reserve. Evidence of the climate crisis in Europe is most evident in the Alps where rock faces are fissuring and glaciers shrinking at an unprecedented rate. But since the first confirmed case in a fur seal on Sunday at Beachport, South Australia – a two-hour trip over the border – people have been worried for their local “pet seal”, known as Sammy. “He’s a great tourist attraction. The locals love him. So, we’d hate to see him get the flu,” Murrell, the president of the Southwest Environment Alliance, a coalition of local environment groups, said. The male southern elephant seal had “kind of adopted the town”, frequenting the foreshore and port, and sometimes the community gardens. In recent weeks, the seal has been spotted near birds presumed to have died from H5N1. Victoria’s first bird flu case was detected in the town, in the far south-west of the state, at the end of July. Since then, the area has become a hotspot, with 17 confirmed events in crested terns, magpies, silver gulls and ravens, according to the federal agriculture department, and many more suspected cases. People were concerned about the carcasses, and the risk of the virus spreading as a result of scavengers eating them. Some have estimated 30 to 40 new sick and dying birds on the beach a day. A spokesperson for Glenelg shire council said the situation was distressing for many in the community. They said the state government’s advice was to leave the dead birds in place, although council had begun removing some where “unacceptable public amenity or safety risks have been identified”. Prof Rob Harcourt, at Macquarie University, said elephant seals like Sammy were “characters” and “the most gregarious animals you’ve ever seen”, which explained why communities named them. Along with Sammy, a regular visitor to Portland, and Neil in Tasmania, many others had gained notoriety, including Humphrey, a three-tonne celebrity who frequented New Zealand coastal towns in the 1980s. Southern elephant seals breed in large colonies, especially on Macquarie Island, Harcourt said. cards.source_text: It’s hard to imagine that the space-crazed general public needed any help getting worked up about astronauts and NASA in the early ’60s. Perhaps the wild popularity of space-related imagery was in part what motivated NASA administrator James Webb to create the NASA Art Program in 1962. Although the program’s handpicked artists weren’t edited or censored in any way, they were briefed on how NASA hoped to be represented, and which emotions their creations were meant to capture—the excitement and uncertainty of exploring these frontiers. NASA was also careful to collect everything the artists produced while participating in the program, from sketches to finished work. In turn, the artists received unprecedented access to launch sites, key personnel, and major events such as Project Mercury and the Apollo 11 Mission. Hundreds of artists, including Andy Warhol, Norman Rockwell, and Laurie Anderson, have brought their unique sensibilities to the project. (Find NASA-inspired art by Warhol and Rockwell above.) (And hey, no shame if you mistakenly assumed Warhol’s 1987 Moonwalk 1 was created as a promo for MTV…) Jamie Wyeth’s 1964 watercolor Gemini Launch Pad includes a humble bicycle, the means by which technicians traveled back and forth between the launch pad and the reinforced-concrete blockhouse where they worked. Photographer Annie Leibovitz offers two views of NASA’s first female pilot and commander, Eileen Collins—with and without helmet. Postage stamp designer, Paul Calle, one of the inaugural group of participating artists, produced a stamp commemorating the Gemini 4 space capsule in celebration of NASA’s 9th anniversary. When the Apollo 11 astronauts suited up prior to blastoff on July 16, 1969, Calle was the only artist present. His quickly rendered felt-tip marker sketches lend a backstage element to the heroic iconography surrounding astronauts Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins. One of the items they carried with them on their journey was the engraved printing plate of Calle’s 1967 commemorative stamp. cards.source_text: It doesn’t quite ring true to call David Bowie a rock star. Ziggy Stardust, the neon synthetic-clad alien alter ego he both created and retired in the early seventies, was, of course, rock stardom outlandishly personified. But then, that was the concept of what turned out to be just one of many personae he deliberately crafted throughout the course of his career. That career was in music, primarily, but looking back on it today, more than a decade after Bowie’s death, it looks more like his medium was culture itself. That’s underscored by his interviews, clips from a variety of which appear in the new video above from YouTube channel T&H Inspiration. Most of T&H’s most popular videos add visuals to speeches by the popularizer of Eastern philosophy Alan Watts, who’s been featured here on Open Culture before. He and Bowie had more in common than it may seem at first, beginning with an Englishness that remained thoroughgoing no matter how far out they ventured into the world. Though Watts’ interest in Buddhism hardly needs stating, it’s worth remembering that he chose to be ordained as an Episcopalian priest rather than as a Buddhist monk. The young Bowie, for his part, very nearly took the latter path, studying under the late Lama Chime Rinpoche, who eventually told him he’d be better off going into the music business. Bowie did so, of course, but with a new “sense of transience and change, which actually became fundamental to my life and my approach to it,” as he put it decades later. That sense manifests even in his early work, but embracing and even pursuing impermanence — the impermanence of sounds, of fashions, of hit records, of life itself — also kept him from getting mired in the irrelevance or auto-kitsch that threatens every superstar. Given the belief that nothing lasts forever, “looking for the source of one’s own being becomes much more important,” as does attempting artistic or intellectual challenges at the very edge of one’s abilities. Alan Watts would probably have agreed. The bigger question is, did he ever hear “Changes”? cards.source_text: A Vocabulary for the Future is a series by the Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona in which notable thinkers reflect on a word of their choosing and are paired with filmmakers who give their writing a visual interpretation. Together, they invite viewers to see familiar language anew, in the hope of laying the groundwork for a better tomorrow. In this instalment, the American theoretical physicist and feminist theorist Karen Barad muses on the nature of touch. Drawing partly on their essay ‘On Touching—The Inhuman That Therefore I Am’ (2012), Barad begins with a puzzle from classical physics: touch, strictly speaking, never happens, since what we feel as contact is only electromagnetic repulsion between atoms that never actually meet. Turning to quantum field theory, they reframe the question entirely. If matter has no stable, self-contained identity – if it is entangled with other matter from the very start – then touch is not a failed meeting between separate bodies, but something already constitutive of what matter is. Paired with visuals by the Barcelona-based digital artist Blanca Rego, the result is a mesmerising set of images that, alongside Barad’s words, turn something as ordinary as touch into a doorway into the deepest questions in physics and philosophy.

Hardly more than a novella, it sits lightly in the hand, but its emotional and aesthetic weight overtips the balance. Thubron began his career as a travel writer and a large part of the action of Passage is set in a vividly but economically evoked Egypt. This is not the teeming Egypt of Cairo or Alexandria, but of the countryside, the villages, and the great immemorial tombs and ancient monuments. The best travel writers know that “abroad” is most convincingly evoked not by awed exclamations at the world’s wonders, but by an attitude of relaxed familiarity. Thubron is obviously an old Egypt hand, or at least has the skill to convince us that he is. The story he tells is both simple and subtle. The main character is Kathleen, an Anglicised Australian actor whose father had emigrated from Slovenia. She is in her 40s, beautiful and gravely ill, and the brief first chapter is a toe-curlingly stark description of an operation on her brain to investigate a tumour which, as we will learn, is incurable. As it happens, Kathleen’s husband, Robert, is himself a brain specialist, and has elected, unwisely, to be present at the operation, “standing as far away as space allows … He finds himself staring speechless into his wife’s brain. It is a turmoil of ink and crimson coils, faintly pulsing under the surgeon’s instrument.” Kathleen is awake, and answering questions that will help the doctor to identify cancerous tissue. Robert and Kathleen’s marriage has gone stale; also, it has a historical blemish, since it was Robert’s younger brother, Alan, who first met Kathleen and fell in love with her when they were both in their teens. cards.source_text: Barbara Cartland was famous for dictating her novels. With a pekingese clamped to her hot pink bosom she would lie back on a library couch and exhale a story about virginal girls taming wayward dukes, damaged airmen or misunderstood surgeons. Meanwhile Miss Savory, Mrs Smith or Mrs Morgan, picked for being unfidgety and sneezeless, would take everything down in immaculate Pitman shorthand. Cartland reckoned on being able to polish off 8,000 words a day. “In this way,” she told one of the many reporters who quizzed her on her astonishing productivity, “the typescript for an 80,000-word novel is finished in a fortnight.” At her peak she was pushing out 23 books a year which added up to 723 in total. Only Agatha Christie and William Shakespeare topped her lifetime sales of 750m. Cartland was a dictator in other ways, too. Husbands, dogs, houses and the local council were all expected to bend themselves to her indomitable will. Resistance, let alone opposition, was futile. The managing director of the company that printed her books suggested that she read Nietzsche on the perceptive grounds that they had a lot of ideas in common. Oddly, he also declared himself madly in love with her. Behind that marshmallowy exterior, all pink chiffon, candyfloss hair and soft, smudgy lines, there lurked sinews of high-tensile steel. Anyone expecting this biography of Barbara Cartland to be an amusing takedown of a monstre sacré along the lines of Craig Brown’s witty 2017 decimation of Princess Margaret will be disappointed. Rather, Matthew Sweet pays his subject the compliment of absolute seriousness, regarding her as a cultural phenomenon whose extraordinary life, stretching the entire 20th century, deserves deep study. Sweet has had unfettered access to the cornucopia of material that Cartland left behind at Camfield Place, the Hertfordshire manor house where she lived until her death in 2000 at the age of 98. Conducting a fingertip search of her letters, scrapbooks and typescripts, Sweet has crafted a generous but clear-sighted account of a woman who was too often reduced to the status of a lazy joke. James Cartland and Son was a Birmingham metalworkers turning out umbrella stands, crocodile-shaped inkwells, shelf brackets shaped like sea monsters and “pharaonic letterboxes embossed with meaningless hieroglyphs”. In her ebullient 1998 debut The New Feminism, Walter hailed Margaret Thatcher as a trailblazer. In this fiercer, bleaker work, she rips into the “glossy language of aspiration feminism”, “the message that the individual woman can do anything she wants if she only has the necessary courage”. That kind of feminism inspired an “explosion of books and films about pioneers and heroines, about bossy women and gutsy girls” which retold the feminist story as “a succession of isolated campaigns, led by outsize individuals”. Instead, Walter advocates for ecofeminism, and for solidarity and sisterhood, “narratives that focus less on how I win on my own, and more on how we thrive together”. She’s serious about that “we”, marshalling stories from across the globe. Walter founded the charity Women for Refugee Women in 2006, directing it for the next 15 years. During that time she was struck by women’s complaints of environmental degradation, their despairing at the “heaps of toxic waste that had grown up behind their homes”. She also saw some feminists who had supported the charity switch their energies to focus solely on British women, who they insisted needed protecting from migrants. cards.source_text: It would have been understandable if Sam Smith wanted to stay in the body shop a little while longer. Their 2023 hit “Unholy,” a spooky infidelity bop featuring Kim Petras, was camp enough (in a “Looking camp right in the eye” kind of way) to inspire a period of mass awareness rare for our fractured pop culture landscape. Smith performed it at the Grammys in a silly top hat with devil horns that nonetheless got freaked-out conservatives hooting and hollering about Satan worship; the reality show The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives, which follows a group of women with varying levels of devotion to the LDS Church as they argue with each other in comfy sweatsuits and huff nitrous at Botox appointments, used it as the theme song for its pilot before switching to a haunted soundalike for the rest of the series. “Unholy” was a moment, Sam Smith’s first American No. 1, and they could have easily rode the wave and kept putting out mildly salacious, medium-corny, maximally synthetic music forever. Instead, for their fourth studio album, Smith has swerved. Hazel Eyes is a collection of sophisticated, romantic songs that tap into jazz, blues, and soul, with production that feels much more organic (and much more interesting) than anything they’ve released before. Past Smith projects have tended to be both uncannily polished and indecisively diverse in genre, and while that approach has produced some monster hits, it also waters down their album artistry. Unique choices and important statements were certainly made on the last two Sam Smith albums, but somewhere between the rote Max Martin/Stargate/Shellback production and the lukewarm Ed Sheeran and Demi Lovato features, one might also a detect a certain unwillingness (or inability) to clock out of their long, grueling shift at the hit factory. No score yet, be the first to add. cards.source_text: Julia Holter has a finger on a pulse and a hand in the ether. Over a decade and a half, the Los Angeles-based musician has written and produced an expansive catalog of celestial yet hummable ambient pop, marrying modern sounds with classical touchstones like Euripides and Hildegard von Bingen, great sprawling compositions that orient the ancient in a neon hall of mirrors. On Materia, the follow-up and companion piece to 2024’s Something in the Room She Moves, she reshapes and reenvisions previously recorded songs alongside new material, and the resulting seven-song odyssey is both slyly glinting and overembellished, dazzling and inscrutable. The record opens with “The Laugh Is in the Eyes,” an asymmetrical, electrified tune that initially feels like a chimera, percussion and melody just barely stitched. Here as elsewhere on the album, instrumental flourishes flash like jewels set in molten metal, momentary glimmers in the strange flow. A flute trills midway through, like something breaking the surface, and a few moments later, the clarinet quavers tentatively before it’s reabsorbed. The layered sounds build like sediment, tall as a canyon, before the song ends abruptly, and the music box piano of album highlight “My Lost One” floats in like a new scene in an extended dream sequence. The lyrics broach surreality. “The news always hits the sea, too,” Holter avers on “The Laugh Is in the Eyes,” and then later: “I still love that day, we chased our tails around.” On “My Lost One,” she sings, “Blossoms in warm kitchens think it’s spring everyday.” No score yet, be the first to add. The title track, which previously appeared on Somewhere in the Room She Moves, is revivified, elasticized and warped nearly beyond recognition as two compositions, “Materia 2” and “Materia 3.” Where the original foregrounds Holter’s soprano like a liturgical relic, barely pinned in place by spare piano, its first doppelganger builds and swells, vocal layers competing like a ghostly peanut gallery. The last iteration, which closes the record, is short, simple, and reverberant, but less sure of itself, and particularly arresting in its use of pauses. It rubs its eyes; it looks down at an ashtray instead of up at a vaulted cathedral. cards.source_text: In 2026, metalcore is experiencing two very different renaissances. While the rock mainstream is being polluted with some of the tamest, schlockiest breakdown-based music of all time, a far more artistically credible variant—mercilessly heavy, authentically hostile, tastefully stylized—has been permeating metalcore’s DIY underground. The genre, which originated as an outgrowth of hardcore before it was captured by the Hot Topic industrial complex, is now being reclaimed by the grassroots community that birthed it. In other words, metalcore is getting good again. The return to metalcore’s sinister roots started in 2023 with a couple of bands, like Balmora and Azshara, referencing the gothic melodeath of Prayer for Cleansing and Undying; then came the early Underoath and Hopesfall worship (I Promised the World, Holder); now there’s a grip of trendy acts working within the pre-Jane Doe Converge paradigm (Killing Me Softly, Crowquill). Living Weapon might be the best band in that latter camp, and their pulverizing debut album, Death in the Family, sets a new high-water mark for metalcore’s burgeoning resistance to SiriusXM’s strain of mainstream complacency. No score yet, be the first to add. Living Weapon also have a leg up on their peers. Four of their five members played in the Boston metallic hardcore bruisers Vein.fm, and that same quartet also makes up the bulk of Fleshwater, the nu-gaze breakouts whose sudden popularity pulled their members’ attention away from hardcore. Vein.fm still haven’t caved to the growing chorus of fans baying for their return, but their members bring the same mixture of apoplectic fury and attention to detail to Living Weapon. Picking up where the 2021 Paradise EP left off, Death in the Family is unrelentingly violent in a way even the singularly intense Vein.fm never were. A lot of that comes down to Living Weapon frontman Jon Lhaubouet: A bassist in his other bands, he growls in this group with a roar that sounds capable of shattering solid stone. His monstrously low screams are the perfect counterbalance to the band’s high-frequency guitar fracas and whiplash-inducing rhythms, ensuring that even when the songs wriggle free of their conventional structures (which is often), Lhaubouet is there to yank them back into place like a dungeon chain. items.summary: Gabriele Taylor, emeritus fellow in philosophy at St. Anne’s College, University of Oxford, has died. Gabriele Taylor was known for her work in moral philosophy, especially moral psychology. She is the author of Pride, Shame, and Guilt: Emotions of Self-Assessment (1985) and Deadly Vices (2006), among other works, which you can learn more about here. She earned her B.Phil at St. Anne’s and taught there for a while, and then moved to Australia to teach at University College of Canberra. She returned to St. Anne’s in 1964 and was a fellow there until her retirement in 1996. Her collected essays, as well as a memoir, will be published next year, edited by her former student, Constantine Sandis. You can listen to an interview with Gabriele Taylor about her life and work, conducted in 2011, here. St. Anne’s College has posted a brief memorial notice here. (via Roger Crisp) The post Gabriele Taylor (1927-2026) first appeared on Daily Nous .

items.title: “Proper education arouses intellectual curiosity”
items.summary: Nathan Ballantyne (ASU) continues his wonderful series of thoughtful, in-depth interviews of philosophers, The Workbench, with a conversation with Paul Gooch (Toronto). . The conversation is wide-ranging, with many amusing anecdotes (including one about the role Richard Taylor’s dog played at a dissertation defense), interesting reflections on various aspects of being a philosophy professor, a discussion of what “Canadian Philosophy” is, and thoughts about the limits of philosophy. Here’s one part of the interview that focused on teaching: Gooch: As Plato pointed out in the Phaedrus, written texts can’t answer your questions, so the conversation is one-way. (Of course, he made the claim about the inadequacy of the written word in writing.) You talk to yourself when you read. That’s not teaching. I was fortunate to learn very early on that teaching isn’t just about getting my own thoughts in order; it’s an interaction that has to take into account the place the student inhabits. Unsurprisingly, another fifty years on I argued that education is best understood as a kind of conversation involving interlocutors—not a surprising view given my interest in Socrates (who wrote nothing himself). Ballantyne: How is that different from the so-called Socratic method? Gooch: It’s certainly different. I don’t mean interrogation to deflate intellectual pretense. Socrates’ victims don’t participate in the dialogue beyond the occasional answer. In fact, I once wrote a poem titled “As I said to Socrates the other day,” which was only a series of Yes, No, Maybe, with ‘Sorry, I’ve got to go now’ as the ending. Proper education arouses intellectual curiosity that asks to know, and the teacher must be open to interrogation as well as the student. items.title: Passage by Colin Thubron review – mortality and memory in a gem of a novel
items.summary: A terminally ill woman makes a final trip to Egypt in an exquisitely wrought portrait of end-of-life reckoning Virginia Woolf said of Middlemarch that it is one of the few English novels written for grown-up people. In the shallow and infantilising age through which we are living, Colin Thubron dares to assume that his readers are adults. Passage is a very beautiful, very moving, authentic work of art. Hardly more than a novella, it sits lightly in the hand, but its emotional and aesthetic weight overtips the balance. Thubron began his career as a travel writer and a large part of the action of Passage is set in a vividly but economically evoked Egypt. This is not the teeming Egypt of Cairo or Alexandria, but of the countryside, the villages, and the great immemorial tombs and ancient monuments. The best travel writers know that “abroad” is most convincingly evoked not by awed exclamations at the world’s wonders, but by an attitude of relaxed familiarity. Thubron is obviously an old Egypt hand, or at least has the skill to convince us that he is. Continue reading...

items.title: The Great Dictator by Matthew Sweet review – the fabulous life of Barbara Cartland
items.summary: A brilliant new biography that does it subject the favour of taking her seriously – even if few else did Barbara Cartland was famous for dictating her novels. With a pekingese clamped to her hot pink bosom she would lie back on a library couch and exhale a story about virginal girls taming wayward dukes, damaged airmen or misunderstood surgeons. Meanwhile Miss Savory, Mrs Smith or Mrs Morgan, picked for being unfidgety and sneezeless, would take everything down in immaculate Pitman shorthand. Cartland reckoned on being able to polish off 8,000 words a day. “In this way,” she told one of the many reporters who quizzed her on her astonishing productivity, “the typescript for an 80,000-word novel is finished in a fortnight.” At her peak she was pushing out 23 books a year which added up to 723 in total. Only Agatha Christie and William Shakespeare topped her lifetime sales of 750m. Cartland was a dictator in other ways, too. Husbands, dogs, houses and the local council were all expected to bend themselves to her indomitable will. Resistance, let alone opposition, was futile. The managing director of the company that printed her books suggested that she read Nietzsche on the perceptive grounds that they had a lot of ideas in common. Oddly, he also declared himself madly in love with her. Behind that marshmallowy exterior, all pink chiffon, candyfloss hair and soft, smudgy lines, there lurked sinews of high-tensile steel. items.title: Feminism for a World on Fire by Natasha Walter review – hope amid the hopelessness
items.summary: A writer and activist links the climate crisis to battles for justice around the world in this vital book It has become increasingly difficult to change our minds, to question our own views or to find common ground with people we disagree with, all of which makes Natasha Walter’s new book both refreshing and exhilarating. In her ebullient 1998 debut The New Feminism, Walter hailed Margaret Thatcher as a trailblazer. In this fiercer, bleaker work, she rips into the “glossy language of aspiration feminism”, “the message that the individual woman can do anything she wants if she only has the necessary courage”. That kind of feminism inspired an “explosion of books and films about pioneers and heroines, about bossy women and gutsy girls” which retold the feminist story as “a succession of isolated campaigns, led by outsize individuals”. items.summary: Even low levels of traffic noise can negate the benefits of listening to natural sounds, researchers say Hearing the trill or whistle of a bird while going about daily life is well known to boost people’s mood.
